title: Optimal time exponent for truth-table decision-tree depth
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
formal:
Determine the real number
\[
\alpha_{\mathrm{ttDT}}=\inf\mathcal E,
\]
where \(\mathcal E\) is the set of real \(a\ge0\) for which one deterministic word-RAM program computes the minimum decision-tree depth of every Boolean function, from its complete truth table of length \(N\), in worst-case time \(O(N^a)\). The input, output, machine and quantifiers defining \(\mathcal E\) are specified below. Give a real answer \(v\) and a complete Lean proof of
\[
|v-\alpha_{\mathrm{ttDT}}|\le\frac1{100}.
\]
This is the user-selected optimal-exponent refinement of the source's broader request for exact sequential time complexity. It measures the exponent in truth-table length \(N=2^n\), not in the number \(n\) of variables. It does not ask for a constant-factor characterization of the entire running-time function, or for the depth of a parallel circuit solving the task. The infimum need not be attained by any one algorithm.
why: This is a basic question in the complexity of optimizing a computational model when its entire input-output behavior is already explicit. It separates knowing every value of a Boolean function from finding its best adaptive query depth. The source establishes polynomial-time solvability and parallel hardness, leaving a substantial gap in the sequential exponent; narrowing that gap would sharpen our understanding of decision-tree optimization and this form of meta-complexity.

importance.reason: A well-motivated meta-complexity question for a fundamental computational model: complete input-output information still leaves an optimization problem whose sharp sequential exponent is unknown in the source. It connects query complexity with algorithm design and separates sequential efficiency from parallel hardness. Its scope is more specialized than a general complexity-class separation, but the full-truth-table setting makes it a clean and consequential test case rather than a parameter adjustment to one algorithm.

sentences: Given the complete truth table of a Boolean function, the task is to compute the minimum worst-case depth of a decision tree evaluating it.
The known sequential upper bound is polynomial in the table length but has an exponent larger than one.
This card asks for the infimum deterministic time exponent in a fixed finite-word random-access model, allowing different uniform algorithms for different candidate exponents.
That exponent separates the cost of optimizing query depth from the query depth itself and from parallel complexity.
An accepted answer must give a real approximation within 1/100 and a complete Lean proof, without assuming that an algorithm attains the infimum.

definitions:
For an integer \(n\ge1\), a Boolean function is a map \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\). Its truth table is the binary array \(X\) of length \(N=2^n\), with positions numbered from zero, in increasing lexicographic order of the input strings; thus the binary expansion of the array index, padded to \(n\) bits, is the argument of \(f\). All \(2^N\) truth tables at each length are valid inputs.

A deterministic decision tree is a finite rooted binary tree with an input-coordinate label in \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) at each internal node, two outgoing edges labeled zero and one, and a Boolean output at each leaf. On input \(x\), it follows the edge labeled \(x_i\) at a node labeled \(i\), and returns the reached leaf's value. It computes \(f\) if that value equals \(f(x)\) for every \(x\). Its depth is the largest number of internal nodes on a root-to-leaf path. Define \(D(f)\) to be the least depth of a tree computing \(f\); it is an integer between zero and \(n\). The required algorithmic output is exactly this integer, not a tree, its number of leaves, an average depth, or an approximation to \(D(f)\).

The computational model is the following explicit deterministic word RAM. Its description contains a finite program, a finite number of named registers, finitely many nonnegative integer constants written in binary, and a positive integer \(d\). These are fixed independently of the input. On an \(n\)-variable instance the word width is
\[
w=d(n+2).
\]
Registers and memory cells hold unsigned integers in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\). The read-only input array contains one truth-table bit per word, in the order just defined. Separate read-only registers give \(n,N,w\). Work memory is an array indexed by all \(w\)-bit addresses, initially zero, and the program's writable registers initially contain zero. There is no other precomputed data. Initial input placement and provision of the three size registers are not charged; examining input values is charged.

One instruction may load a fixed constant reduced modulo \(2^w\), copy a register, read one input cell at a register address, read or write one work-memory cell at a register address, or apply one of the following operations to at most two register operands: addition, subtraction or multiplication modulo \(2^w\); unsigned integer quotient or remainder with a nonzero divisor; bitwise AND, OR, XOR or complement on \(w\) bits; logical left or right shift by the unsigned value of a register; equality or unsigned-order comparison. Shifted-out bits are discarded, vacated bits are zero, and a shift by at least \(w\) gives zero. Conditional branches use the comparison result and jump to one of the finitely many program labels. A halt instruction returns one designated register. Every instruction costs one step, including every memory access, comparison, branch and halt. Instructions have fixed register operands and labels in the finite description; arbitrary code, tables or computations cannot be supplied as a constant-time instruction. A zero divisor or out-of-range input-array access is a failure, not a permitted oracle result. Addresses for work memory are always \(w\)-bit unsigned integers. There is no randomness, advice, real arithmetic, unbounded-precision unit-cost operation, parallelism or access to a tree oracle. All preprocessing must use the same charged instructions.

For a program \(A\), including its declared \(d\), let \(\tau_A(X)\) be its step count if it halts normally on \(X\), and \(+\infty\) if it does not halt or incurs a failure. Let \(f_X\) denote the function with table \(X\). Precisely,
\[
\mathcal E=\left\{a\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}:\
\exists A\ \exists C\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\
\forall n\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall X\in\{0,1\}^{2^n},\quad
\tau_A(X)\le C(2^n)^a\ \land\ A(X)=D(f_X)\right\}.
\]
The output equality requires normal halting with that value. The exponent and program are chosen before all input lengths and tables. The multiplicative constant \(C\) is independent of them. This all-length convention is equivalent to allowing a finite initial range of exceptional lengths and changing the fixed program and constant there. Different candidate exponents may use different finite programs and word-width constants.

The set \(\mathcal E\) is nonempty and bounded below. In this model the elementary input-reading lower bound and the source's sequential upper bound give
\[
1\le\alpha_{\mathrm{ttDT}}\le\log_2 3.
\]
The upper endpoint is an infimum bound: the known running time includes a polynomial factor in \(n\), and need not belong to \(O(N^{\log_2 3})\) itself. The source states its sequential bound on a random-access machine; the finite word width, instruction set and explicit input layout above make that convention precise. No exact equivalence of running times on all machine models is asserted.
answer_criterion:
Supply an unambiguous real value \(v\) and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that \(|v-\alpha_{\mathrm{ttDT}}|\le1/100\). Alternatively, supply a certified real interval \([\ell,u]\) containing \(\alpha_{\mathrm{ttDT}}\) with width at most \(1/50\). The interval's midpoint is then an admissible real approximation. The answer need not be an integer or an exact closed form. Merely repeating the defining infimum without establishing its location does not determine the requested value.

Bounds must control the full algorithm class. An upper bound \(\alpha_{\mathrm{ttDT}}\le u\) can be certified by showing that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) some fixed program and constant achieve correct worst-case time \(C N^{u+\varepsilon}\) on every truth table; the program and constant may depend on \(\varepsilon\). No single program attaining exponent \(u\) is required. A lower bound \(\ell\le\alpha_{\mathrm{ttDT}}\) must exclude every exponent \(0\le a<\ell\): for every candidate program and constant, some length and table must exceed its proposed \(C N^a\) bound or violate exact correctness. A lower bound for one algorithm does not give this conclusion.

Both sides needed for the numerical tolerance must be proved. A conditional lower bound settles only the conditional statement unless the extra assumption is also established. Faster evaluation of a supplied decision tree, computation from a succinct circuit, approximation to \(D(f)\), optimization of leaf count, and parallel-circuit depth are different targets. The numerical tolerance applies to the optimal time exponent; the algorithms in its definition must still compute \(D(f)\) exactly.

User explicitly chose optimal exponent of deterministic time in truth-table length and numerical1/100 tolerance. No need to assume the infimum is attained or to return integer approximation. Exponent c is quantified before one uniform program and all lengths; per-length hardcoded algorithms cannot exploit the definition. Full-table array uses one bit per word, source-consistent up to logarithmic packing factors; fixed word-width constant belongs to the program. The finite instruction set excludes unit-cost operations on arbitrarily large integers.

Well-definedness audit: every exact program must inspect every input-table position along the all-zero table run, because changing an unread bit yields a nonconstant function with depth>0. Thus worst-case time>=N in this model. The source random-access dynamic program stores polynomially many O(n)-bit indices/values and runs in O(3^n poly(n)) on a sufficiently large fixed word width, hence E contains every real exponent above log2(3). This proves finite infimum interval [1,log2(3)] but not attainment. These audit details are not public solution hints.
